questions.prompt: An owner says most of her clients buy 10-class packs and few are on memberships. What's the most useful thing to ask next?

options.text: Which social channels her pack buyers follow her on
How often pack buyers come in and whether they renew
Whether she'd like to stop selling class packs at all
How long she has been teaching Pilates as an instructor

questions.reveal: Pack buyers who come often are the natural candidates for a membership. Their visit pattern tells you how much recurring revenue she's leaving on the table.

questions.prompt: Why does filling every spot matter so much in a reformer studio?

options.text: Reformer clients only ever pay for unlimited memberships
Reformers have to be rebooked by staff after every class
Insurers require each reformer studio to run at capacity
A class can only hold as many people as there are machines

questions.reveal: Capacity is set by the number of reformers. Revenue grows by filling those spots and keeping privates booked, not by squeezing more people in.

questions.prompt: A privates-heavy owner asks whether memberships would really earn her more. What do you do?

options.text: Ask about her spots, private vs group mix and teacher pay
Tell her memberships always earn more than privates do
Say that's a question only her accountant can answer
Tell her to switch every private client to a membership

questions.reveal: The answer depends on her numbers. Ask for them and work through the trade-off with her instead of giving a general answer.

questions.prompt: What does the training say separates a side project from a profitable Pilates studio?

options.text: A large Instagram following and a branded mobile app
Offering every class format in one studio, all week
A recurring base, full spots and a working intro funnel
Paying every teacher a salary rather than per class

questions.reveal: Instructor pay and rent are the big costs. A studio covers them with recurring members, full spots and intro offers that turn into members.

questions.prompt: A boutique owner says a new chain studio just opened down the street. What's your best next step?

options.text: Tell her chains usually close within their first year
Move on, since competitors aren't part of the demo
Ask what makes her studio different and who it's for
Offer a discount so she can lower her prices to match

questions.reveal: Boutique owners compete on attention and fit. Her answer tells you which features to show, like screening, privates and personal follow-up.

questions.prompt: According to the training, what's the catch with clients who come through third-party apps like ClassPass?

options.text: Studios earn less per booking and few become members
Their bookings can't be added to the studio roster
The studio has to pay a fee before each such class
Those clients are barred from buying a membership

questions.reveal: The apps bring first-timers, but studios earn less per visit and few of those visitors convert. Owners weigh the exposure against that cost.

questions.prompt: An owner says, “We're a Lagree studio.” Which follow-up shows you know the format?

options.text: “So mostly mat classes, with a bigger room per class?”
“Do your teachers hold comprehensive certification?”
“Do you mostly teach classical work on the Cadillac?”
“How many Megaformers do you run in each class now?”

questions.reveal: Lagree is taught on its own machine, the Megaformer. Like reformers, the number of machines sets each class's capacity.

questions.prompt: What does a comprehensive Pilates certification cover?

options.text: Mat only, usually earned in a single weekend course
Mat plus Reformer, Cadillac, Chair and the Barrels
Reformer only, with a focus on group class cueing
Lagree on the Megaformer, plus studio management

questions.reveal: Comprehensive training covers mat and the full apparatus. The National Pilates Certification Program asks for at least 450 hours.

questions.prompt: An owner gives teachers and friends and family a discount, set up today as a fake free membership. What do you show?

options.text: A price rule that gives a tagged group its discount
A promo code each person types in at every checkout
A separate drop-in price she edits by hand per client
A gift card she reloads for each person every month

questions.reveal: Tag the group, and a price rule applies their discount automatically. Nobody has to ask for a code.

questions.prompt: An owner says new clients must not book a class while injured. What do you show first?

options.text: A survey sent the week after each client's first class
A note the instructor types into each client by hand
A checkout question asking if the client is injured
A waiver that clients sign at the front desk on paper

questions.reveal: The studio writes its own checkout questions. An injury answer can tag the client so the instructor sees it on the roster.

questions.prompt: What does Spot Filler use to decide who gets a last-minute spot message?

options.text: New leads who haven't bought anything at the studio
Past attendance at that kind of class and time of day
Clients ranked by how much they've spent this year
Anyone on the studio's newsletter list, all at once

questions.reveal: Spot Filler targets clients who've attended that kind of class before. That's why it suits established studios more than new ones.

questions.prompt: An owner with limited reformers wants late cancellations to get a credit, not a refund. What do you show?

options.text: A promo code she sends to anyone who cancels late
A refund she reverses by hand on the client's card
A new class pack she sells to people who cancel late
The cancellation setting that gives credit back

questions.reveal: The studio chooses what a cancellation gets: nothing back, a credit or a refund. Credit back keeps the money in the studio.

questions.prompt: A pre-open owner's website won't be ready for two months, but she wants to sell founding memberships now. What do you show?

options.text: A paper sign-up sheet that she enters into Momence later
A waitlist that opens on the day the website goes live
A promo code she can hand out at her next pop-up event
The membership's own purchase link for her Instagram

questions.reveal: Every membership has its own purchase page and link. She can sell from Instagram or a link-in-bio before the site exists.

questions.prompt: In Momence, what's the difference between a location and a room?

options.text: A room has an address and a location sits inside it
A location is a physical place; a room sits inside it
They're the same thing with two different names
Locations are for classes and rooms for appointments

questions.reveal: A location is physical and can hold an address. A room is a space inside a location.

questions.prompt: A founder runs pop-ups at a club using an event platform. She says, “It's not my own CRM.” What's the point to make?

options.text: Event platforms can't take any card payments online
She should stop running pop-ups until her studio opens
Each Momence checkout adds the guest to her own list
Momence can import contacts from any event platform

questions.reveal: Every Momence checkout creates or updates a contact, with a signed waiver. She keeps the attendee list for her opening.

questions.prompt: A traveling instructor got a bad review from a client who went to the wrong venue. What do you focus on?

options.text: Setting up each venue so clients see where they booked
Turning off reviews so a bad one can't be posted again
Running every class through one virtual Zoom location
Asking her to stop teaching at more than one venue

questions.reveal: Her pain is clients going to the wrong place. Each venue set up as its own place shows clients exactly where they booked.

questions.prompt: An owner asks when a reformer integration will be ready. You don't know. What do you say?

options.text: “I don't have a date, and I won't promise one.”
“It's coming next quarter, so you're all set.”
“Every other platform is far behind us on that.”
“We don't plan to build that, so it won't happen.”

questions.reveal: Don't guess a roadmap. Saying you don't have a date keeps the prospect's trust.

questions.prompt: A long-time MindBody owner says, “It works, I've used it for years.” What's the best response?

options.text: Tell her it looks outdated next to every other system
Agree and end the call, since she sounds happy with it
Skip discovery and go straight to pricing and contract
Ask what she'd keep, then what slows her or clients down

questions.reveal: Acknowledge what her system does well, then find where it costs her time or clients. Never knock the competitor.

questions.prompt: Which need does the training list for Pilates studio software?

options.text: One app per teacher, separate from the studio's own
Ad-free booking pages that hide all class prices
Privates and group classes run in the same system
Manual waitlists the owner approves before class

questions.reveal: Pilates studios sell privates and classes side by side. They want both in one system, with spot booking, waitlists and cancellation rules.

questions.prompt: A solo instructor with no studio yet says Momence sounds like more than she needs right now. What do you do?

options.text: Show every add-on so she sees the full value of it
Build only what she needs and say if an add-on can wait
Tell her to call back once she has opened a studio
Offer a deep discount before you know her budget

questions.reveal: Build the quote around what she'll use now. Saying an add-on isn't worth it yet builds trust.
